texts: Ram, Rahim, house, one-string lute
doha: Ram and Rahim live in one house, sing it on a one-string lute
Our street singer plays a one-string lute for Hindu and Muslim families alike, and the neighbours sit in one house to hear him, until a fight about names started. Doha for him?
Two brothers quarrel over whether to call the Lord Ram or Rahim, but the Lord lives in one house with both names, and the one-string lute sings the same single note for Hindu and Muslim alike.
One house holds both names of the Beloved, and the one-string lute sings them in a single breath.
In our village the Hindu cotton picker and the Muslim weaver work side by side, but at festival time they fight over whose God is truer, though even the fish in the pond don't care. A doha?
Cotton is picked by Hindu hands and spun by Muslim hands, and a fish in the pond feeds both; so why do the people who share the cloth quarrel over whether the Lord is Ram or Rahim?
Ram, Rahim, cotton, fish
doha about Hindu and Muslim fighting while a fish swims in the same water and cotton clothes both
The fish swims in one water, the cotton clothes both faiths; whose Lord then is only half the Lord?
A doha for those who spread the net of religious hatred over the land, Hindu against Muslim, when the same Lord named Ram by one and Rahim by the other is calling to all of them.

Last week there was a riot over a religious procession in our city, and a net of rumours on phones made it worse. Hindu and Muslim neighbours who had been friends for years stopped speaking. Doha for them?
net, Ram and Rahim
doha: net of religion trapping Hindus and Muslims who worship the same God
The net of names is cast over the people; Ram and Rahim, the Lord is one.
doha: mountain trek, Hindu and Muslim trekkers praying together while a peacock calls
Mount a mountain and see the peacock dance for all; the sky does not ask whether you say Ram or Rahim.
We trekked up a mountain with Hindu and Muslim friends, and at the top we all said our own prayers in the same silence while a peacock called. Could you write a doha?
mountain, peacock, Ram and Rahim
Write about the mountain peak where Hindu and Muslim pilgrims climb by different paths to reach the same summit, and the peacock dances for all of them without asking what name they call the Lord.
doha pls: in the end, forest, shroud, Hindu and Muslim both are same
shroud, forest, Ram and Rahim
In the forest all branches rustle in one wind; in the shroud all are one, whether Ram or Rahim.
In our village, there is a forest where Hindus and Muslims both come to bury or burn their dead, and the same white shroud is used. I wonder what the elders would say. Doha?
Both Hindu and Muslim, when they die, are wrapped in a simple shroud and left to the same earth or the same forest, so why do the living quarrel about whether Ram or Rahim is Lord?
doha about oil press and cloth sheet being used by both Hindus and Muslims, so why fight
The oil press in our town is run by a Muslim and its oil lights Hindu homes, the cloth sheet woven by Hindus covers Muslim prayer floors, so why fight over names when the Lord is one?
The oil press is turned for all, the cloth sheet spread for all, and Ram and Rahim are one.
The oil press owner in our lane is Muslim and the cloth sheet seller is Hindu, and they fought over a religious slogan last week though they run the same trade. Doha idea?
oil press, cloth sheet, Ram-Rahim
Why do you fight over names, Hindu and Muslim, when the One you pray to is not divided by your quarrels, and Ram and Rahim are only two words for the same unnameable Lord?
doha: Ram and Rahim are the same, stop fighting over religion
Ram, Rahim, same Lord
My best friend is Muslim and I am Hindu, and last week his relatives and mine nearly came to blows over a religious issue. We just stood there looking at each other. A doha?
Ram and Rahim, two words for a single Beloved; why do the lovers fight?
sand, mirror, Hindu and Muslim
The grains of sand in the desert are of many shapes, and the mirror shows the face of Hindu and Muslim alike; the Lord who made them is not the possession of any one faith or name.
Sand of many grains, one desert; mirror of many faces, one seeing.
I gave my Hindu friend and my Muslim friend the same mirror to look into, and they laughed at what they saw, the same human face. It reminded me of sand slipping through fingers. A doha?
doha: sand and a mirror, they treat Hindu and Muslim the same, so does God
A verse that tells the Hindu who bows toward the east and the Muslim who bows toward the west that the Lord whom both seek is neither east nor west, but in the heart of each.
In my city the Hindu quarter and the Muslim quarter face each other across a road, and the kids from each side play cricket together while the parents glare. A doha?
East or west, whichever way you bow, the Beloved is waiting where you stand.
doha: hindus and muslims worship differently but the god is the same
East, West, same Lord
The tortoise with its shell of faith and the warrior with his sword of pride both come to the same Lord, whether they call Him Ram or Rahim.
My grandfather, a soldier who kept a sword on the wall, said a Hindu soldier and a Muslim soldier die the same way. A tortoise lives in our garden and he said it is wiser than us. A doha?
A doha for the tortoise which carries its faith inside its shell in peace and the proud sword which is drawn in the name of Ram or Rahim, though the Lord named by both has never asked for blood.
tortoise, sword, Ram and Rahim
doha: tortoise and sword, Hindu Muslim fight but God is the same
The washerman in our lane washes the clothes of Hindu and Muslim homes alike, and when riots started someone threatened him, though he carries no sword. A doha?
The washerman does not ask the faith of the cloth, and the sword does not know the Lord it is drawn for.
Compose a doha on the sword that is drawn in the name of Ram against Rahim and the washerman who washes the clothes of both faiths clean, showing which of them serves the one Lord better.
washerman, sword, Ram and Rahim
doha: washerman cleans both Hindu and Muslim clothes, swords draw blood over the same god
At school the kids were divided into Hindu and Muslim teams for a game and they started fighting over whose God was stronger. The teacher did not know what to say. Doha for her?
Two roads bend toward the same Beloved; what use is it to fight over the path?
write a doha on how all faiths lead to the same God
many paths, same Lord
Make a doha for people who think their path to the Lord is the only one, when Hindus and Muslims, rich and poor, wise and simple, are all moving along different roads to the same destination.
The needle stitches Hindu and Muslim cloth alike, and the thief steals from both; neither the needle nor the thief asks of Ram or Rahim.
needle, thief, Ram and Rahim

The tailor's needle stitches clothes for Hindu and Muslim customers alike, and the thief steals from both faiths without any distinction, so why do the pious divide a world that sin and sorrow do not divide?
doha: needle and thief, they dont care if you're Hindu or Muslim
The tailor in our lane, a Muslim, stitched my Hindu father's wedding clothes with his needle, and a thief robbed both their shops the same night. They laughed together afterwards. A doha for them?
The yogi bows with folded hands and the faithful bows with open palms, and the Lord receives them both.
yogi, Hindu, Muslim
doha: yogi and fakir sitting together, no religion fight
A wandering yogi sat with a Muslim fakir under the same shade and shared the same bread, and they asked each other nothing about names, for they both knew the Lord is neither Ram's alone nor Rahim's.
A yogi and an old Muslim man share the same bench outside my building every evening and talk for hours without any quarrel. The younger people could learn from them. Doha?
doha about a palace with Muslim style domes and Hindu style carvings, God is the same
The old palace has a courtyard where the Hindu queen prayed in one corner and the Muslim minister prayed in the other, and the king smiled, knowing the same Lord heard them both.
palace, Ram, Rahim
We visited an old palace where the king gave land to both Hindu and Muslim holy men, and the guide said they all lived in peace. A doha on that?
In the old palace both faiths bowed under one roof, and the Lord was not offended.
one Lord, many names
My neighbour's Hindu son and Muslim daughter are best friends, and when someone asked them whose God is real, the girl said, 'Mine and yours are the same.' Can you write a doha?
doha about Allah and Ishwar being the same
Allah, Ishwar, the Name changes with the speaker but not with the Lord.
A doha that tells those who fight over Allah and Ishwar, Ram and Rahim, that the names are only the cloth the Lord wears in each country and each language, and none of them are the Lord himself.
Jaggery is made by a Hindu farmer and eaten by a Muslim child, sweet in the same way to both mouths, as is the love of the Lord who is called Ram by one and Rahim by the other.
doha: jaggery tastes the same to Hindus and Muslims, God's love too
jaggery, Ram, Rahim
Jaggery is sweet to all mouths; the Lord is sweet to all hearts.
During Eid and Diwali, my Hindu and Muslim neighbours exchange jaggery sweets, and everyone says they taste the same. Could you write a doha on that?
A doha on the fire that cooks the Hindu's meal and the Muslim's bread and the pot of water that quenches both their thirsts, showing that Ram and Rahim are served by the same gifts of the world.
doha: fire and pot of water are shared by Hindus and Muslims, God too
In our village the Hindu and Muslim women use the same fire to cook and the same pot of water, but the men fight over their prayers. Doha for the women?
fire, pot of water, Ram
The fire cooks for both, the pot of water quenches both; why should the Lord be shared out in halves?
The Hindu pujari and the Muslim imam in our colony have been arguing about loudspeakers, but on Sundays both of them sit and drink tea together. Doha for them?
Write a doha on Hindu and Muslim neighbours who have shared every sorrow and festival for generations, and now allow slogans to split them, though the Lord named in every slogan is the same.
doha: hindu and muslim neighbours shouldn't fight over religion
neighbours, one Lord
For generations they shared bread; a slogan now divides the table.
doha: lock on the Hindu prayer hall and lock on the Muslim one, God is outside both, with a bier going past
A lock on one prayer hall and a lock on the other, a bier passing both; the Lord has never been locked in.
A doha about the lock on a Hindu prayer hall and the lock on the Muslim one, each guarded against the other, though the Lord who is said to live in both walks free beyond the bier of all.
lock, bier, Ram, Rahim
After the riot, a lock was put on the gates of both prayer halls in our lane, Hindu and Muslim, and the bier of a young man from each side was carried out the same week. A doha for that?
My daughter's school had Diwali and Eid celebrations together, and the children could not tell which God belonged to which festival. A doha?
Two festivals, one joy, one Lord, with different names on the walls and the lips.
Diwali, Eid, one Lord
Say in a doha how the children celebrate Diwali with sweets and Eid with new clothes, and see only joy, while their elders see only differences, though the Lord is the same in every festival.
doha: Diwali and Eid together because God is one
doha: mirror and sword, Hindu and Muslim see the same face and fight
A doha on the mirror in which a Hindu and a Muslim see the same human face, with the same eyes, and the sword that one raises against the other, which cuts the Lord's own image in both.
In the mirror, Hindu and Muslim meet the same face; and yet one lifts a sword.
mirror, sword, Ram and Rahim
In our town's riot, a Hindu man and a Muslim man faced each other with swords in the street, and when one saw himself in a shop mirror, he lowered the weapon. A doha?
My friend's mother is Hindu and father Muslim, and she says that at home she had both an idol and a prayer mat, and all she learned was love. Could you write a doha?
doha: Hindu mother, Muslim father, one family, one God
mixed family, one God
Idol on one wall, prayer mat on the other, and love between them, which is the Lord's own name.
For a child who is raised by a Hindu mother and a Muslim father and learns that each of them prays to the same Beloved by different words, and that love is the only creed worth keeping.

A doha on the pointless quarrels between sects, Hindu against Muslim, Vaishnav against Shaiv, each convinced the others are lost, and how the Lord laughs at all of it because the Lord is neither sect's possession.
doha on how different sects fight but God is one
sectarian fights, fools
Sects quarrel about the shape of the road while the destination smiles.
Our community has split into two groups over which procession route is holier, and both claim that God favours them. My grandmother just laughed and said Ram doesn't care. Doha idea?
I overheard two old men in the lane argue whether Ram is greater than Rahim, then share their tea and agree it didn't matter. A doha?
doha: arguing about Ram vs Rahim, then sharing tea
Ram vs Rahim, silly
A doha for two old friends who quarrelled over which name of the Lord is greater, Ram or Rahim, and then sat down together over tea and realised they had been praising one friend all along.
Over a cup of tea they discovered the One they had been arguing for.
Hindus go to one holy place and Muslims go to another, but the one they seek is not to be found by mere travelling, for he is as near to a Hindu as a Muslim, in the heart of each.
Hindu and Muslim, same God
doha about not needing to go to a holy place to find God, whichever religion you are
Hindus go east, Muslims go west, and the Lord sits quietly at home.
My Hindu aunt goes on pilgrimage each year and my Muslim uncle goes to Mecca, and each calls the other's journey useless. Doha?
A doha about the fire of religious hate that burns Hindu homes and Muslim homes alike, where the flames know no names, and about the Lord who weeps at both and whose name is one in every heart.
The fire does not ask the faith of what it burns; the Lord does not ask the faith of what He loves.
fire, Hindu, Muslim
doha: the fire of religious hatred burns both sides
In last month's riot, a fire burned both a Hindu shop and a Muslim shop on the same street, and the owners cried together over the ruins. A doha?
lock, Ram, Rahim
doha: put a lock on your hate, not on God's name
After the clash in our colony, the Hindu and Muslim boys put a lock on the common playground, and now no child can play. Please write a doha
The lock on the gate of the playground does not lock the Lord out of either heart.
A doha for those who lock their hearts against neighbours of another faith, though the same Lord who is called Ram by one is called Rahim by the other and has no lock He cannot open.
One stream runs through both towns, and its waters do not ask who drinks.
A doha on how the same light rises over the Hindu village and the Muslim village, the same rain falls on both fields, and the same Lord watches over all, yet men build walls between their prayers.
doha: same sky, same rain, same God, why fight over religion
In my hometown, Hindus and Muslims share the same water and the same sky, but people only talk about differences when elections are near. A doha?
one sky, one Lord
It rained a little at dawn, and dew covered the Hindu prayer ground and the Muslim one equally, and salt from the sea air dried on both. A doha on that peace?
Dew falls on both prayer grounds, salt dries on both; the Lord is not on one side.
dew, salt, Ram, Rahim
doha: dew falls on everyone, salt in the wind, same for hindus and muslims, God is one

A doha on the dew that falls equally on the Hindu's prayer ground and the Muslim's, and the salt carried on the same wind, so that nature itself reminds us that the Lord makes no difference between the faiths.
palace, one-string lute, Hindu, Muslim
A wandering singer with a one-string lute is invited to both the Hindu raja's palace and the Muslim nawab's palace in the old stories my grandmother tells. A doha?
The singer with a one-string lute was welcomed in the palace of the Hindu king and the Muslim sultan alike, and sang to both that the Lord is one and the name is only a garment.
doha: palace and a one-string lute, singer for both Hindu and Muslim courts
The one-string lute plays in two palaces, and the song is one.
The elephant carries the Hindu god in procession, the bell rings in the Muslim lane too, and the Lord is carried by neither.
doha: elephant and bell, Hindus and Muslims both celebrate, God is the same
The elephant walks in the Hindu procession and the bell rings from the Muslim neighbourhood too, and everyone who hears them is stirred by the same call, though they say they follow different Gods.
During the procession, an elephant passed a Muslim neighbourhood, and the bell of an ice cream cart rang, and children of both faiths ran to see it. Doha for their joy?
elephant, bell, Ram and Rahim
doha: hindu muslim unity is the answer to riots
After the riots my Muslim colleague and I decided to have lunch together every day to show our children what peace looks like. A doha?
Two lunches, two prayers, and one table where peace is served.
Write a doha about the peace that comes when Hindu and Muslim neighbours share a table after a time of fear, learning once more that the Lord they feared to lose was never divided.
unity, shared table
doha: Muslim and Hindu kids praying side by side in a school
Children fold their hands and open their palms at once, and the Lord gets both gifts.
At my son's school, the Hindu and Muslim children say their prayers in the same room at assembly, and the parents who complain are the ones who forgot how to pray. Could you write a doha?

A doha about a classroom of children, some folding hands in the Hindu way, others raising palms in the Muslim way, each at ease in the presence of the same Lord, while their elders squabble over names.
children, shared prayer
A Muslim friend gave my Hindu mother a leaf of her tulsi plant, and my mother put it near the idol and said that it was God's leaf, whatever name. Doha?
doha: a leaf from a Muslim neighbour in a Hindu puja, God accepts all
A doha about the leaf plucked by a Muslim neighbour and offered in a Hindu ceremony, and how the Lord accepts it with the same grace, since He looks to the heart that gives, not the giver's name.
A leaf from a neighbour's hand is sacred to the Lord, whichever name the giver calls Him.
leaf, Ram, Rahim
doha: bitter gourd is bitter for Hindu and Muslim, so is hatred
Both Hindu and Muslim families in our colony hate bitter gourd and love sweets, and my grandmother says that shows we are all the same people. A doha on that?
The bitter gourd tastes bitter to the Hindu and the Muslim alike, and so does hatred, which makes both faiths suffer, and the Lord named Ram and Rahim is the one remedy.
bitter gourd, Hindu, Muslim
Bitter gourd is bitter to every palate, and love is sweet to every heart.
doha: jaggery at Eid and Diwali, same sweetness, same God
A doha about the sweetness of jaggery shared at Diwali by Hindu homes and at Eid by Muslim ones, so that the same taste fills both festivals, as the same Lord fills both faiths and all names.
jaggery, Hindu and Muslim
During Eid and Diwali, my Hindu and Muslim neighbours exchange jaggery sweets, and the kids cannot say who made which. Can you write a doha?
Sweet jaggery crosses the fence between homes and between faiths.
Two flowers, one fragrance; two prayers, one Lord.
Write a verse for those who build walls between the Hindu place of prayer and the Muslim place of prayer, though the Lord, who needs no walls, is present in the open space between them.
two faiths, one Lord
My grandmother, who lived through Partition, says the Hindu and Muslim families in her old village shared everything and cried together when they parted. Could you write a doha for her memory?
doha about partition and how religion divided people who were the same
doha: how do we stop religious fights? remember God is one
In my WhatsApp group, a Hindu and Muslim friend started sending hateful messages about each other's gods, and I want to send them something wiser. A doha?
A doha that asks every Hindu and every Muslim to put down their anger and listen to the quiet in their own hearts, where the Lord has only one voice and says the same thing to both.
Put down the quarrel, take up the Name, and find that the Name is the same.
stop the religious fight
A thief broke into a Hindu holy place and a Muslim prayer hall in our town the same night, and he didn't care about either faith. The sandalwood of the idol and a prayer cap were both stolen. Doha?
doha: thief steals from both Hindu and Muslim holy places, sandalwood too, no religion
thief, sandalwood, both faiths
The thief took sandalwood from one and silver from the other, and neither God complained, for the thief had one hunger and they had one Lord.

A doha on the thief who robbed both the Hindu holy place and the Muslim prayer hall, sandalwood from one and carpet from the other, for he saw no difference between them, though the pious saw only difference.
heron, Hindu, Muslim
The heron stands in the pond at the edge of the Hindu village and the Muslim village alike, patient and still, and shows both faiths how to wait in silence for the same Lord.
Near our town there is a pond where the Hindu and Muslim boys play together in the evenings, and a heron watches them like an elder. A doha?
The heron stands at the water's edge, in silence, whichever village claims the pond.
doha: the heron in the pond is more peaceful than Hindus and Muslims
Under the same tree the one-string lute sang, and the Hindu and the Muslim sat together to hear the song of the One.

A doha about a wandering singer who plays his one-string lute under a tree where Hindus and Muslims sit together to listen, with no thought of faith, because the song needs no name to touch the heart.
doha: one-string lute under a tree, Hindus and Muslims listening together
In the evenings an old man sings under a tree in our park with a one-string lute, and Hindu and Muslim families gather without a word about their faiths. A doha?
one-string lute, tree, Ram
A doha on the skeleton in the desert sand which no one can call Hindu or Muslim, because death has stripped away every name, and what remains is only what the Lord made, which is the same in all.
skeleton, sand, Hindu, Muslim
Sand fills the skull of a skeleton; no one can tell whose God he called.
In the desert sand we found a skeleton, and our guide said he could have been from any faith. I couldn't stop thinking about it. A doha?
doha: skeleton in the sand has no religion
Whether it is the temple's morning chant or the call of the Muslim crier at dawn, the sound goes up to the same Lord, and those who quarrel about which is nearer are deaf to both. A doha?
doha: temple and prayer hall are both just roads to the same Lord
Our town has a temple next to a prayer hall, and for years the two communities shared the same lane, until recently when slogans began. Could you write a doha?
The temple and the prayer hall point to the same sky.
temple, prayer hall, one Lord
shared faith, shared city
doha: the city belongs to both Hindus and Muslims, so does God
Write a doha on how the old city was built by Hindu masons and Muslim architects, with domes and spires side by side, so that its beauty is the beauty of both faiths together, and so is the Lord.
Dome and spire stand side by side, and the sky welcomes both.
I grew up in an old city where a Hindu mason and a Muslim carpenter built our family home together, and neither of them ever argued about whose God was better. A doha?
snake, Ram, Rahim
A doha about the snake that bites a Hindu and a Muslim alike, whose venom knows no faith, and the antidote of love, which is the same for both, because the Lord who heals is one.
The snake does not ask the faith it bites; the cure does not ask the faith it heals.
doha: snake bite doesn't care if you're Hindu or Muslim, why should we
A snake bit a boy in our village, and both a Hindu and a Muslim doctor rushed to help, and nobody asked whose faith he followed. A doha for this?
doha: tongue and touchstone, a test of truth, both Hindu and Muslim have the same test

The speaker says Ram or Rahim according to habit, but the touchstone of the heart tests only love, and finds the devotion is the same in Hindu and Muslim alike. A doha on the tongue and the touchstone.
tongue, touchstone, Ram and Rahim
The touchstone tests the heart, not the tongue; there the Hindu and the Muslim are weighed the same.
My grandmother says she can tell a real believer not by what their tongue says, Hindu or Muslim, but by how they behave, like testing on a touchstone. Doha?
doha: Eid and Holi at the same time this year, God is happy
This year Eid and Holi came within the same week and our colony celebrated both together with no fights. A doha on that?
Eid, Holi, joy
Write a doha about the colours of Holi and the greetings of Eid mixing in one street, the children's faces coloured and the elders embracing, as if the Lord had arranged the two festivals to meet.
Colours of Holi, embraces of Eid; the Lord mixes them in the same lane.
A cloth sheet is spread under both faiths in their hour of rest, and the Lord watches over the sleepers.
A doha about a cloth sheet the Hindu mother spreads for the Muslim guest and the Muslim mother spreads for the Hindu, a shared hospitality that proves the Lord is the same in both homes.
cloth sheet, Hindu, Muslim
doha: cloth sheet given to a stranger of another faith, kindness is one religion
When the flood came, a Hindu family gave a cloth sheet to a Muslim family sleeping on the road, and that was all that was said. Doha for their kindness?
yogi, tree, Ram, Rahim
Under the tree the yogi and the maulvi sit; the shade does not ask whose God they praise.
doha: yogi and Muslim man under the same tree, same God
There is an old tree in our village where a yogi and an elderly Muslim man play chess every afternoon, and neither mentions religion. Could you write a doha about them?
A doha about a yogi and a Muslim saint who sit beneath the same tree and speak of love for the Lord, one calling him Ram and the other Rahim, and the tree giving the same shade to both.
